frequency_question: How often do domestic structural friction points (specifically sub-national state government opposition in federal systems) prevent the formal renewal of expiring transboundary water treaties?
membership_rule: Includes international water treaties involving federal states where a distinct sub-national region's consent is structurally required or practically mandatory for implementation; excludes unitary states where central government fiat bypasses regional friction.

cases.name: Colorado River Basin Salinity Agreement extensions (US-Mexico)
Teesta River interim water sharing draft (India-Bangladesh)

coverage_note: 5 named major federal transboundary water friction cases; captures the relevant class of structural veto interference.
known_gaps: Does not exhaustively cover minor municipal-level water sharing pacts, focusing solely on sovereign bilateral treaties.
skeleton: Total comparable bilateral water treaty renewal attempts involving federal structural friction points since 1970 divided by those successfully concluded despite regional veto friction.
multiplier: 4 hits out of 5 comparable instances where sub-national or structural institutional friction was present.
validity_reason: Constitutional structures governing federal-state relations in transboundary resource management evolve slowly over decades.
